{{Short description|Mathematical theorem, used in calculus}}
{{calculus|expanded=integral}}
In [[mathematics]], '''integrals of inverse functions''' can be computed by means of a formula that expresses the [[antiderivative]]s of the [[inverse function|inverse]] <math>f^{-1}</math> of a [[continuous function|continuous]] and invertible function {{nowrap|<math>f</math>,}} in terms of <math>f^{-1}</math> and an antiderivative of {{nowrap|<math>f</math>.}}  This formula was published in 1905 by [[Charles-Ange Laisant]].<ref name=Laisant>{{cite journal|last=Laisant|first=C.-A.|title=Intégration des fonctions inverses|year=1905|pages = 253–257|issue=4|volume=5|journal=[[Nouvelles annales de mathématiques, journal des candidats aux écoles polytechnique et normale]]}}</ref>

==Statement of the theorem==
Let <math>I_1</math> and <math>I_2</math> be two [[interval (mathematics)|intervals]] of {{nowrap|<math>\mathbb{R}</math>.}} 
Assume that <math>f: I_1\to I_2</math> is a continuous and invertible function. It follows from the [[intermediate value theorem]] that <math>f</math> is [[strictly monotone]]. Consequently, <math>f</math> maps intervals to intervals, so is an open map and thus a homeomorphism. Since <math>f</math> and the inverse function <math>f^{-1}:I_2\to I_1</math> are continuous, they have antiderivatives by the [[fundamental theorem of calculus]].

Laisant proved that if <math>F</math> is an antiderivative of {{nowrap|<math>f</math>,}} then the antiderivatives of <math>f^{-1}</math> are:
<math display="block">\int f^{-1}(y) \, dy = y f^{-1}(y) - F \circ f^{-1}(y)+C,</math>
where <math>C</math> is an arbitrary real number. Note that it is not assumed that <math>f^{-1}</math> is [[Differentiable function|differentiable]].

[[File:FunktionUmkehrIntegral2.svg|thumb|Illustration of the theorem]]

In his 1905 article, Laisant gave three proofs.  
=== First proof ===
First, under the additional hypothesis that <math>f^{-1}</math> is [[Differentiable function|differentiable]], one may differentiate the above formula, which completes the proof immediately. 
=== Second proof === 
His second proof was geometric.  If <math>f(a) = c</math> and {{nowrap|<math>f(b) = d</math>,}} the theorem can be written: 
<math display="block">\int_c^d f^{-1} (y) \, dy + \int_a^b f(x) \, dx = bd - ac .</math>
The figure on the right is a [[proof without words]] of this formula.  Laisant does not discuss the hypotheses necessary to make this proof rigorous, but this can be proved if <math>f</math> is just assumed to be strictly monotone (but not necessarily continuous, let alone differentiable). In this case, both <math>f</math> and <math>f^{-1}</math> are Riemann integrable and the identity follows from a bijection between lower/upper [[Darboux sum|Darboux sums]] of <math>f</math> and upper/lower Darboux sums of {{nowrap|<math>f^{-1}</math>.}}<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Key" /> The antiderivative version of the theorem then follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus in the case when <math>f</math> is also assumed to be continuous. 
=== Third proof ===
Laisant's third proof uses the additional hypothesis that <math>f</math> is differentiable.  Beginning with {{nowrap|<math>f^{-1}(f(x)) = x</math>,}} one multiplies by <math>f'(x)</math> and integrates both sides.  The right-hand side is calculated using integration by parts to be {{nowrap|<math display="inline">xf(x) - \int f(x) \, dx</math>,}} and the formula follows.
=== Details ===
One may also think as follows when <math>f</math> is differentiable. As <math>f</math> is continuous at any <math>x</math>, <math display="inline">F:= \int_0^x f(t) \, dt</math> is differentiable at all <math>x</math> by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Since <math>f</math> is invertible, its derivative would vanish in at most countably many points. Sort these points by <math> ... < t_{-1} < t_0 < t_1 < ... </math>. Since <math>g(y):= yf^{-1}(y) - F\circ f^{-1}(y) + C</math> is a composition of differentiable functions on each interval <math>(t_i, t_{i + 1})</math>, chain rule could be applied
<math>g'(y) = f^{-1}(y) + y/f'(y) - f\circ f^{-1}(y).1/f'(y) + 0 = f^{-1}(y)</math> to see <math>\left.g\right|_{(t_i, t_{i + 1})}</math> is an antiderivative for <math>\left.f\right|_{(t_i, t_{i + 1})}</math>. We claim <math>g</math> is also differentiable on each of <math>t_i</math> and does not go unbounded if <math>I_2</math> is compact. In such a case <math>f^{-1}</math> is continuous and bounded. By continuity and the fundamental theorem of calculus, <math display="inline">G(y) := C + \int_0^y f^{-1}(t) \, dt</math> where <math>C</math> is a constant, is a differentiable extension of <math>g</math>. But <math>g</math> is continuous as it's the composition of continuous functions. So is <math>G</math> by differentiability. Therefore, <math>G = g</math>. One can now use the fundamental theorem of calculus to compute <math display="inline">\int_{I_2} f^{-1}(t) \, dt</math>.

Nevertheless, it can be shown that this theorem holds even if <math>f</math> or <math>f^{-1}</math> is not differentiable:<ref name=Key/><ref name="Bensimhoun">{{cite arXiv|eprint=1312.3839|class=math.HO|first=Michael|last=Bensimhoun|title=On the antiderivative of inverse functions|year=2013}}</ref> it suffices, for example, to use the Stieltjes integral in the previous argument.  On the other hand, even though general monotonic functions are differentiable almost everywhere, the proof of the general formula does not follow, unless <math>f^{-1}</math> is [[absolutely continuous]].<ref name=Bensimhoun/>


It is also possible to check that for every <math>y</math> in {{nowrap|<math>I_2</math>,}} the derivative of the function <math>y \mapsto y f^{-1}(y) -F(f^{-1}(y))</math> is equal to {{nowrap|<math>f^{-1}(y)</math>.}}{{Citation needed|date=April 2020}} In other words:
<math display="block">\forall x \in I_1 \quad \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{(x+h)f(x+h)- x f(x) -\left(F(x+h)-F(x)\right)}{f(x+h) - f(x)} = x.</math>
To this end, it suffices to apply the [[mean value theorem]] to <math>F</math> between <math>x</math> and {{nowrap|<math>x+h</math>,}} taking into account that <math>f</math> is monotonic.

==Examples==
#Assume that {{nowrap|<math>f(x) = \exp(x)</math>,}} hence {{nowrap|<math>f^{-1}(y) = \ln(y)</math>.}} The formula above gives immediately <math display="block">\int \ln(y) \, dy = y\ln(y)-\exp(\ln(y)) + C= y\ln(y)-y + C.</math>
#Similarly, with <math>f(x) = \cos(x)</math> and {{nowrap|<math>f^{-1}(y) = \arccos(y)</math>,}} <math display="block">\int \arccos(y) \, dy = y\arccos(y) - \sin(\arccos(y))+C.</math>
#With <math>f(x) = \tan(x)</math> and {{nowrap|<math> f^{-1}(y) = \arctan(y)</math>,}} <math display="block">\int \arctan(y) \, dy = y\arctan(y) + \ln \left|\cos(\arctan(y))\right| + C. </math>

==History==
Apparently, this theorem of integration was discovered for the first time in 1905 by [[Charles-Ange Laisant]],<ref name="Laisant"/> who "could hardly believe that this theorem is new", and hoped its use would henceforth spread out among students and teachers. This result was published independently in 1912 by an Italian engineer, Alberto Caprilli, in an opuscule entitled "Nuove formole d'integrazione".<ref name="Caprilli">[https://ebooks.library.cornell.edu/cgi/t/text/pageviewer-idx?c=math&cc=math&idno=00420001&view=image&seq=5&size=100 Read online]</ref> It was rediscovered in 1955 by Parker,<ref name=Parker>{{cite journal|last=Parker|first=F. D.|title=Integrals of inverse functions|date=Jun–Jul 1955|pages = 439–440|volume=62|journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]]|doi=10.2307/2307006|issue=6|jstor=2307006}}</ref> and by a number of mathematicians following him.<ref>It is equally possible that some or all of them simply recalled this result in their paper, without referring to previous authors.</ref> Nevertheless, they all assume that {{math|''f''}} or {{math|''f''{{i sup|−1}}}} is [[Differentiable function|differentiable]]. 
The general version of the [[theorem]], free from this additional assumption, was proposed by Michael Spivak in 1965, as an exercise in the ''Calculus'',<ref name=":0">[[Michael Spivak]], ''Calculus'' (1967), chap. 13, pp. 235.</ref> and a  fairly complete proof following the same lines was published by Eric Key in 1994.<ref name=Key>{{cite journal|last=Key|first=E. |title=Disks, Shells, and Integrals of Inverse Functions|date=Mar 1994|pages = 136–138|volume=25|journal=[[The College Mathematics Journal]]|issue=2|doi=10.2307/2687137|jstor=2687137 }}</ref>
This proof relies on the very definition of the [[Darboux integral]], and consists in showing that the upper [[Darboux integral|Darboux sums]] of the function {{math|''f''}} are in 1-1 correspondence with the lower Darboux sums of {{math|''f''{{i sup|−1}}}}.   
In 2013, Michael Bensimhoun, estimating that the general theorem was still insufficiently known, gave two other proofs:<ref name="Bensimhoun"/> The second proof, based on the [[Stieltjes integral]] and on its formulae of [[integration by parts]] and of [[homeomorphic]] [[integration by substitution|change of variables]], is the most suitable to establish more complex formulae.

==Generalization to holomorphic functions==
The above theorem generalizes in the obvious way to holomorphic functions:
Let <math>U</math> and <math>V</math> be two open and simply connected sets of {{nowrap|<math>\mathbb{C}</math>,}} and assume that <math>f: U \to V</math> is a [[biholomorphism]].  Then <math>f</math> and <math>f^{-1}</math> have antiderivatives, and if <math>F</math> is an antiderivative of {{nowrap|<math>f</math>,}} the general antiderivative of <math>f^{-1}</math> is
<math display="block">G(z)= z f^{-1}(z)-F\circ f^{-1}(z)+C.</math>

Because all holomorphic functions are differentiable, the proof is immediate by complex differentiation.
